lessons.title: Whole-Body Listening
objectives: Show good listening with eyes, ears and a still body
Follow a two-step instruction
prerequisites: Can follow a simple one-step instruction
explanation: Good listening uses your whole body. Your eyes look at the speaker. Your ears are ready. Your mouth is quiet. Your hands and feet are still.
When someone gives an instruction, listen to the whole thing before you start. "Pick up the red block and put it in the box" has two steps: pick up, then put in.
If you forget, it's okay to ask: "Can you say that again, please?" Asking is part of good listening.

vocabulary.meaning: pay attention to sounds and words
words that tell you what to do

examples: "Wash your hands, then sit at the table." — two steps.
Simon Says is a listening game: only move when you hear "Simon says".

story.title: Pala's Treasure Map
story.text: Pala the dolphin told the fish: "Swim to the big rock, then look under the shell." Little Fin swam off before Pala finished and got lost. The other fish listened to the whole instruction. They swam to the rock, looked under the shell — and found shiny treasure! Fin came back and asked, "Can you say that again, please?"

activities.prompt: Good listeners look at…
"Clap your hands, then touch your nose." Put the steps in order

lessons.title: Conversation Catch
objectives: Take turns speaking and listening in a conversation
Use polite words and full sentences
prerequisites: Can listen attentively for a short time
explanation: A conversation is like playing catch with a ball. One person speaks (throws), the other listens (catches) and then answers (throws back).
If two people talk at once, the ball drops! Wait for a pause before you speak. If you need to interrupt, say "Excuse me".
Using full sentences helps people understand: not just "Water!" but "May I have some water, please?" Polite words make conversations kind.

vocabulary.meaning: people talking and listening in turns

examples: "What did you do today?" "I painted a picture. What did you do?"
"Excuse me, may I say something?"

story.title: The Dropped Ball
story.text: Momo and Kiko were playing catch. Momo threw the ball, but Kiko was busy talking and — thud! — it dropped. "Talking is like catch too," laughed Momo. "If we both talk at once, the words drop!" So they took turns: one talked, one listened, then they swapped.

activities.prompt: In a conversation we…
Most polite way to ask for juice:
options: May I have some juice, please?

activities.prompt: Match the polite words
It is kind to wait for a pause before speaking.

thinking: How do you feel when someone talks over you?

lessons.title: Who, What, Where, When, Why?
objectives: Use question words to find out information
Ask a follow-up question in a conversation
explanation: Question words help us find out different things. Who asks about a person. What asks about a thing or action. Where asks about a place. When asks about time. Why asks for a reason. How asks about the way something happens.
Good listeners ask follow-up questions. If a friend says "I went to the beach", you could ask "What did you see there?" That shows you are interested.
Questions end with a rising voice and, in writing, a question mark.

vocabulary.meaning: a question that asks more about what someone just said

examples: Where do penguins live? (a place)
Why do leaves fall in autumn? (a reason)

story.title: The Curious Reporter
story.text: Zuri the zebra became a reporter for the Globe Garden News. She interviewed Tara: "Who are you? Where do you live? Why are you so slow?" Tara smiled: "I'm Tara. I live by the pond. I'm slow because my shell is heavy — but it keeps me safe!" Zuri wrote it all down.

activities.prompt: Match the question word to what it asks
"I went to the zoo." A good follow-up question:
Which question asks for a reason?
Asking follow-up questions shows you are listening.

thinking: Which question word is the hardest to answer? Why?

lessons.title: My Show and Tell
objectives: Describe an object using several details
Speak clearly to a small group
explanation: In show and tell, you bring something special and talk about it. Good describing tells what it looks like, feels like, what it is used for and why it is special to you.
When speaking to a group: stand tall, look at your audience, speak loudly enough for the back row, and don't rush.
The audience has a job too: listen, then ask a question or give a kind compliment.
examples: "This is my wooden elephant. It is brown and smooth. My grandmother brought it from Kerala."
Audience question: "How old is it?"

story.title: Bolt's Shiny Bolt
story.text: Bolt brought a tiny metal bolt for show and tell and mumbled, "This is a bolt." Nobody heard. Bolt tried again, standing tall: "This is a silver bolt. It is cold and heavy. It holds my arm on. Without it, I couldn't wave!" Everyone clapped — and asked lots of questions.

activities.prompt: When speaking to a group, look at…

activities.prompt: Order a show and tell

lessons.title: Say It Step by Step
objectives: Give clear spoken instructions in the right order
Check that the listener understood
explanation: Instructions tell someone how to do something. Good instructions are in order and use sequence words: first, next, then, finally.
Start each step with a "bossy verb" — an action word: fold, cut, pour, stir. Keep each step short and clear.
Watch your listener. If they look confused, slow down, show them, or ask: "Does that make sense?"

vocabulary.meaning: steps telling how to do something
an action word that starts an instruction

examples: First, fold the paper in half. Next, fold the corners down. Finally, fold the edges up — a paper boat!
"Does that make sense? Shall I show you?"

story.title: The Peanut Butter Robot
story.text: Kiko told Bolt, "Make a sandwich." Bolt stood still. "Put peanut butter on bread," said Kiko. Bolt put the whole jar on the bread! Kiko laughed and tried again: "First, open the jar. Next, use a knife to spread a little on one slice. Then put the other slice on top." Bolt made a perfect sandwich.

activities.prompt: Order the instructions for brushing teeth
Which is a bossy verb?
Good instructions can be in any order.
If your listener looks confused, you should…

thinking: Why did Bolt get it wrong the first time?
Is it easier to give instructions or to follow them? Why?
speaking: Teach someone how to make a paper boat (or another simple thing) using only spoken instructions — no touching!

units.title: Explaining My Thinking

lessons.title: I Think… Because…
objectives: Explain an opinion or answer with a reason
Agree or disagree politely and build on others' ideas
explanation: Good thinkers explain their ideas: "I think the bridge fell because it was too thin." The word "because" shows your reason.
In discussions, people may disagree — and that's okay. Disagree with the idea, not the person: "I see what you mean, but I think…"
You can also build on someone's idea: "I agree with Asha, and I'd add that…" This makes group thinking stronger.
examples: "I think we should play inside because it's raining."
"I disagree, because we have umbrellas and the rain is light."

story.title: The Great Pet Debate
story.text: The Heart Harbor friends had to choose a class pet. "A fish, because it's quiet," said Momo. "I see what you mean, but I think a rabbit, because we can hold it," said Zuri. "I'd add that a rabbit needs lots of care — can we manage that?" said Tara. They listened to every reason before deciding together.

activities.prompt: Which sentence gives a reason?
options: I like dogs because they are friendly.

activities.prompt: Most polite way to disagree:
options: I see what you mean, but I think…

activities.prompt: Match the sentence starter to its purpose

thinking: Can two people both have good reasons and still disagree?
Have you ever changed your mind after hearing someone's reason?
speaking: Choose a question ("Is summer better than winter?") and explain your answer to someone with two reasons.

lessons.title: Hook, Points, Close
objectives: Structure a presentation with a hook, main points and a conclusion
Use voice and gesture to engage an audience
explanation: A strong presentation has three parts. The hook grabs attention: a question, surprising fact or short story. The main points (usually two or three) give the information. The conclusion sums up and leaves the audience thinking.
Delivery matters as much as content. Vary your voice (louder, softer), pace (slow down for important bits) and use pauses for effect. Gestures can show size, shape or importance.
Use notes with key words, not full sentences, so you talk to the audience rather than reading. Practise aloud at least three times.

vocabulary.meaning: a talk that shares information with an audience
a movement of the hands or body that adds meaning

examples: Hook: "What animal can sleep for up to three years? A snail!"
Pause before revealing a surprising answer.

story.title: Nova's Nervous Talk
story.text: Nova had to present about the planets and wrote every word on paper. On the day, Nova read it fast, eyes down, and nobody remembered anything. Next time, Nova used three key-word cards, started with "Did you know a day on Venus is longer than its year?", and practised with a mirror. The class was spellbound.

activities.prompt: Order a presentation
Which is the best hook?
options: Today I will talk about bees.
What would happen if all the bees disappeared?

activities.prompt: Your notes should be…
Pausing can make an important point stand out.

Should a presentation include your opinion? When?

lessons.title: Discussion Roles
objectives: Take on a discussion role effectively
Help a group reach a reasoned decision
explanation: Groups think better when people take roles. The leader keeps the group on task. The summariser sums up what has been said. The challenger asks "Are we sure? What's the evidence?" The includer invites quiet members to speak.
Good discussions have ground rules: one person speaks at a time; respond to ideas, not people; everyone gets a chance.
To reach a decision, list options, weigh reasons for each, and agree on the best — or find a compromise.

vocabulary.meaning: an agreement where each side gives a little
agreed rules for how a group works

examples: Includer: "Ravi, we haven't heard from you — what do you think?"
Summariser: "So far we have two ideas: a garden and a library corner."

story.title: The Silent Member
story.text: In a group choosing a class project, three loud voices argued while Leela stayed quiet. Tara, the includer, asked, "Leela, what do you think?" Leela suggested combining a garden with reading benches. Everyone loved it. "We nearly missed the best idea," the group realised.

activities.prompt: Match the role to its job
A good ground rule:
options: One person speaks at a time

activities.prompt: A compromise means…

Is it always good to reach agreement? When might disagreement be useful?

lessons.title: How a Debate Works
objectives: Explain the structure of a formal debate
Construct an argument and a rebuttal
explanation: A debate is a structured argument about a motion, such as "This house believes homework should be banned." The proposition argues for the motion; the opposition argues against it.
Each argument needs a claim, a reason and evidence. A rebuttal responds directly to the other side's argument, showing why it is weak or incomplete.
Debaters may be assigned a side they do not personally agree with. This builds the skill of understanding different viewpoints — a key part of fair thinking.

vocabulary.meaning: the team arguing for the motion
a response that challenges an argument

examples: Motion: "Schools should have longer breaks." Proposition: breaks improve focus. Opposition: longer breaks mean longer school days.
Rebuttal: "The opposition says focus doesn't improve, but the study we cited shows…"

story.title: Arguing the Other Side
story.text: Kiko was told to argue AGAINST more playtime — the opposite of what Kiko believed. Kiko grumbled, then researched and found real reasons: shorter lunches mean earlier home time, more time for clubs. After the debate, Kiko said, "I still prefer playtime, but now I understand why some people disagree."

activities.prompt: Match the term to its meaning
A rebuttal should…
Debaters sometimes argue for a side they don't believe.
Order an argument

thinking: Is it honest to argue for something you don't believe? What can you gain from it?
What is the difference between winning a debate and being right?
speaking: Prepare and deliver a two-minute speech for one side of a motion, then a one-minute rebuttal of the other side.

project.title: Family Debate Night

assessment.prompt: Strong debate arguments include evidence.

lessons.title: Listening Critically
objectives: Summarise a spoken argument accurately
Evaluate the evidence and techniques used by a speaker
explanation: Active listening means not just hearing but processing: noting the main points, asking clarifying questions, and summarising fairly.
Critical listening adds evaluation: Is the claim supported by evidence? Is the speaker using emotion instead of reasons? What is left out? Who benefits if I believe this?
You can respect a speaker and still question their argument. Fair-minded listeners give credit to good points even when they disagree overall.

vocabulary.meaning: listening carefully to understand and respond

examples: Summarising: "So your main point is that recycling is not enough on its own?"
Evaluating: "That was an emotional story, but is it typical?"

story.title: The Miracle Water Advert
story.text: A loud advert promised: "Drink Sparkle Water and become a genius!" with a famous actor smiling. Zuri listened critically: no evidence, a celebrity instead of a scientist, and an impossible promise. "Great music," she said, "but zero proof."

activities.prompt: Which is a clarifying question?
options: When you say "most people", how many do you mean?

activities.prompt: A celebrity selling a product is mainly using…
You can respect a speaker and still question their argument.
Match the question to what it checks

thinking: Why is critical listening especially important today, with so many videos and ads?
How can you tell if you are disagreeing because of evidence or just because you dislike the speaker?
speaking: Listen to a short speech or advert, summarise it in two sentences, and give a fair evaluation.

lessons.title: Speeches That Shaped History
objectives: Analyse the context, purpose and techniques of historic speeches
Apply techniques in an original speech
explanation: Some speeches are remembered because they captured a historic moment. Jawaharlal Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech, delivered at midnight as India became independent on 15 August 1947, used powerful imagery: "At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom."
Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" speech (1963) used repetition (anaphora) to build emotion and vision for civil rights in the United States.
Analysing a speech means asking: What was the context? Who was the audience? What was the purpose? Which techniques were used, and how effective were they?

context.text: Nehru delivered "Tryst with Destiny" to the Constituent Assembly on the night of 14–15 August 1947. King delivered "I Have a Dream" at the March on Washington on 28 August 1963. Texts and recordings of both are preserved.

vocabulary.meaning: repeating words at the start of successive clauses
the situation in which a speech is given
the rhythm and flow of speech

examples: Anaphora: "I have a dream… I have a dream…"
Imagery: "when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom."

story.title: The Midnight Speech
story.text: On a humid August night in 1947, members of the Constituent Assembly gathered in Delhi. Outside, crowds waited. As midnight approached, Nehru rose to speak of a "tryst with destiny". Millions later heard or read those words, and they are still quoted at every Independence Day.

Repeating "I have a dream" is an example of…

lessons.title: Socratic Questioning
objectives: Use types of Socratic questions to deepen dialogue
Contribute to a seminar that builds shared understanding
explanation: Socrates, an ancient Greek philosopher known mainly through the writings of his student Plato, explored ideas through questioning rather than lecturing.

Socratic questions include: clarifying ("What do you mean by…?"), probing assumptions ("What are we assuming?"), asking for evidence ("How do we know?"), exploring viewpoints ("How might someone disagree?") and implications ("If that's true, what follows?").
In a Socratic seminar, the goal is not to win but to understand a text or question more deeply together. Participants refer to the text, build on each other, and are willing to change their minds.

context.text: Socrates (c. 470–399 BCE) left no writings; our knowledge of him comes chiefly from Plato and Xenophon, whose portrayals differ.

vocabulary.meaning: something accepted as true without proof
a consequence that follows from an idea

examples: "When you say a law is unjust, what makes a law just?"
"If honesty is always right, what about lying to protect someone?"

story.title: The Question That Wouldn't Go Away
story.text: A seminar began with "Is it ever right to break a rule?" One student said "Never." Another asked, "What about a rule that harms people?" A third asked, "Who decides if a rule is harmful?" By the end, nobody had a final answer — but everyone understood the question far better than when they started.

activities.prompt: Match the question to its type
pairs: What do you mean by fair?
What are we taking for granted?
What would follow if that were true?

activities.prompt: The goal of a Socratic seminar is to win the argument.
Most of what we know about Socrates comes from…
A good seminar participant…
options: builds on others and refers to the text

thinking: Is there value in a discussion that ends without an answer?
Why might Socrates have preferred questions to lectures?
speaking: Facilitate a 15-minute family seminar on a big question, using at least four types of Socratic question.

Socrates lived in ancient…
